name: The Standing Wave

detectability.signature: faint luminous overlays of past events threaded with the electromagnetic whisper of century-old transmissions

proximity: Faint ghost images of ancient ships flicker at the edge of vision
Audio systems pick up subaudible murmurs resembling crowded harbors
contact: Crew hear complete transmissions broadcast generations ago, clear as live traffic
Brief vivid impressions of decks, weather, and voices belonging to other eras
prolonged_exposure: Immersion in replayed scenes blurs recollection of which memories are one's own
Mild but persistent temporal disorientation requiring rest away from the zone

phenomena: Visible echoes of past events replaying on a fixed schedule
Radio signals arriving before being sent at the boundary layer
Debris briefly existing in two timeframes simultaneously
opportunities: Data valuable to historical and scientific institutions
Listening access to communications from vanished civilizations
Archaeological significance for locating long-lost fleets
known_incidents: The first survey wing mistook the echo fleet for an active armada and withdrew under silent running for three days
description: The Standing Wave is a modest sphere of softly glowing space where the past refuses to settle. Within its fourteen-hundred-kilometer radius, translucent vessels glide routes they finished sailing millennia ago, and the black is never quite empty. Observers describe the light as lantern-glow through deep water.

Every eleven minutes the resonance crests and the scene replays: the same convoy, the same weather of solar wind, the same final maneuver. Signals bleed backward at the boundary, letting patient listeners catch transmissions seconds before their sources emit them. Nothing here can harm a hull; the danger is entirely to the sense of now.

The survey wing's three-day silent withdrawal became a gentle joke among cartographers, but the discovery rewrote regional history. Historians traced the echoed fleet to a diaspora thought wholly lost, and archives now queue for listening time. The wave has repeated faithfully since before any living institution existed and shows no sign of stopping.

Research platforms anchor permanently at a respectful distance, siphoning history eleven minutes at a time. Pilots use it as a landmark and a lesson in humility, since their own traffic will presumably join the program eventually. Travelers are advised to enjoy the show and remember afterward which century they belong to.
